claims.text: The baseline is an as-deposited nanocrystalline FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating on a conventional metal substrate.
Controlled post-deposition annealing can induce a bimodal grain-size distribution in the FeNiCrCoCu coating.
The annealing-induced bimodal grain structure stabilizes nanoscale grain boundaries during high-temperature sliding.
Stabilized nanoscale grain boundaries promote controlled dynamic recrystallization during high-temperature sliding.
Controlled dynamic recrystallization facilitates formation of a uniform, continuous protective oxide layer.
A continuous protective oxide layer reduces material loss from the coating.
The annealed bimodal-grained FeNiCrCoCu coating will have a significantly lower wear rate than the as-deposited nanocrystalline coating.
The annealed coating will develop a continuous protective oxide film during high-temperature sliding.
The as-deposited nanocrystalline coating will exhibit higher wear than the annealed coating.
The as-deposited coating will form a less uniform oxide layer than the annealed coating.
The proposed mechanism applies to sliding wear at 500–700°C.
The proposed mechanism applies under loads representative of high-temperature service environments.
Changes in substrate type or substantially different thermal or mechanical regimes may alter the operative wear mechanisms.
Prior high-entropy-alloy coating studies support grain-boundary stabilization as a means of enhancing oxide-film formation.
High-entropy-alloy coatings on low-cost substrates can be economically preferable to bulk high-entropy alloys.
Failure to obtain either a statistically significant wear-rate reduction or a continuous protective oxide film in the annealed coating would falsify the hypothesis.
